descriptions.CSC-261: Surveys the central ideas of artificial intelligence, including search, knowledge representation, reasoning under uncertainty and machine learning. Students implement several techniques and discuss their limits.
descriptions.CSC-262: Examines how computers extract information from images, covering image formation, filtering, features and recognition. Programming projects apply the mathematics to real photographs.
descriptions.CSC-281: Alumni working in computing visit to talk about their careers and the choices that led to them. Students reflect on their own plans in short written responses.
descriptions.CSC-282: A short, hands-on course in the tools and habits of working programmers on Unix systems. Topics include the shell, build tools, debugging and idiomatic C.
descriptions.CSC-301: Teaches the design and analysis of efficient algorithms, including divide and conquer, greedy methods, dynamic programming and graph algorithms. Students prove correctness and running-time bounds and meet the limits of efficient computation.
descriptions.CSC-312: Students learn how programming languages work by building interpreters and compilers. Topics include parsing, type checking, code generation and runtime support.
descriptions.CSC-313: A deeper study of operating system design for students who have completed the systems course. Sample entry: the advising guide names this course, and the catalog does not yet describe it.
descriptions.CSC-315: Considers the social consequences of algorithmic decision making and the responsibilities of those who build such systems. Sample entry: the advising guide names this course, and the catalog does not yet describe it.
descriptions.CSC-324: Students work in teams on a substantial software project for a real client. The course covers requirements, design, testing, version control and the practices that keep a team productive.
descriptions.CSC-326: Students who have completed the software design course lead project teams in it. They practice mentoring, planning and technical leadership and reflect on what works.
descriptions.CSC-341: Studies what can and cannot be computed, using finite automata, grammars and Turing machines. The course closes with complexity classes and the question of which problems are efficiently solvable.
descriptions.CSC-395: An advanced special-topics course on the theory and design of modern programming languages. Students study type systems and language semantics and apply them in programming projects.
descriptions.MAT-123: The first half of a two-semester path through single-variable calculus that reviews functions along the way. Covers limits, derivatives and their applications at a measured pace.
descriptions.MAT-124: Completes the two-semester path through first-semester calculus. Covers integration and its applications while continuing to strengthen work with functions.
descriptions.MAT-125: Introduces mathematical modeling with functions for first-year students. Linear, exponential and periodic models are fitted to data and used to answer questions from the sciences and social sciences.
descriptions.MAT-131: A first course in calculus covering limits, derivatives, integrals and the fundamental theorem that links them. Applications are drawn from the natural and social sciences.
descriptions.MAT-133: Continues single-variable calculus with techniques and applications of integration, sequences and series. The course ends with an introduction to functions of several variables.
descriptions.MAT-208: Covers the mathematics that computer science depends on: logic, proof, sets, relations, counting and graphs. Students practice writing rigorous arguments and connect each topic to programs.
descriptions.MAT-215: Introduces vectors, matrices, linear systems, vector spaces and linear transformations. Students move between computation and proof and see applications in geometry and data.
descriptions.MAT-218: A transition to proof-based mathematics through discrete topics such as combinatorics, graph theory and number theory. Students learn to read, write and critique proofs.
descriptions.MAT-220: Studies ordinary differential equations and the systems they model. Analytical, qualitative and numerical methods are developed side by side.
descriptions.MAT-222: A transition to proof-based mathematics organized around the foundations of analysis and algebra. Students learn to read, write and critique proofs.
descriptions.MAT-306: Students build and analyze mathematical models of problems from biology, economics and physics. Projects emphasize choosing assumptions, testing a model against data and communicating results.
descriptions.MAT-313: Studies algorithms for approximating solutions to mathematical problems, including root finding, interpolation, integration and linear systems. Students analyze error and implement the methods.
descriptions.MAT-314: A second course in applied mathematics whose topic changes from year to year. Recent themes include optimization, partial differential equations and dynamical systems.
descriptions.MAT-316: A rigorous treatment of the real numbers, sequences, continuity, differentiation and integration. Students write proofs of the theorems that calculus relies on.
descriptions.MAT-317: Continues the study of analysis with a topic chosen by the instructor, such as measure theory, complex analysis or metric spaces. Students present proofs at the board and write up a final project.
descriptions.MAT-321: Introduces groups, rings and fields and the structure-preserving maps between them. The emphasis is on abstraction and proof.
descriptions.MAT-322: Continues the study of abstract algebra with a topic chosen by the instructor, such as Galois theory, representation theory or algebraic number theory. Regular problem sets lead to a final presentation.
descriptions.MAT-330: Students carry out data science projects from question to communication, working with messy, real data sets. Topics include data wrangling, visualization, modeling and reproducible workflows.
descriptions.MAT-335: Develops probability theory with calculus: random variables, distributions, expectation and limit theorems. The course lays the groundwork for mathematical statistics.
descriptions.MAT-336: Builds the theory of statistical inference on probability, covering estimation, hypothesis testing and regression. Students connect the theory to data analysis.
descriptions.MAT-444: A capstone seminar for senior majors on a topic that draws together several areas of mathematics. Students read advanced material and present it to one another.
descriptions.STA-209: Introduces statistical thinking with real data: study design, exploratory analysis, inference and regression. Students use statistical software throughout and complete a data analysis project.
descriptions.STA-230: Introduces the tools of data science, including data wrangling, visualization and reproducible analysis in a programming environment. Students complete projects with data they collect or find.
descriptions.STA-270: Introduces methods for predicting outcomes from data, such as regression, classification and resampling. Students compare models and learn to judge how well predictions generalize.
descriptions.STA-309: Teaches how to plan experiments and analyze their results, including factorial and blocked designs. Students design and run an experiment of their own.
descriptions.STA-310: Extends regression to multiple predictors, categorical outcomes and correlated data. Students fit, check and interpret models in case studies.
descriptions.STA-330: Students carry out data science projects from question to communication, working with messy, real data sets. Topics include data wrangling, visualization, modeling and reproducible workflows.
descriptions.STA-335: Develops probability theory with calculus: random variables, distributions, expectation and limit theorems. The course lays the groundwork for mathematical statistics.
descriptions.STA-336: Builds the theory of statistical inference on probability, covering estimation, hypothesis testing and regression. Students connect the theory to data analysis.
descriptions.STA-340: Introduces the Bayesian approach to inference, in which prior beliefs are updated with data. Students fit models by simulation and compare the results with classical methods.
descriptions.STA-350: Covers advanced topics in statistical modeling, such as generalized linear models and models for dependent data. Students work through the theory and apply it to substantial data sets.
descriptions.STA-370: Studies the main methods of machine learning, both supervised and unsupervised, with attention to the mathematics behind them. Students implement and evaluate methods on real data.
